finding_dispositions.note: The cited sentences are replaced by clauses that state the reason: the third interpretation's Collect follows the review's rewrite at Chrysostom's continual watch, its Secret stands with Aquinas's directio in opere, Mk 11:23 is replaced by the Communion's own words with Bede's reading of the mountain as the devil driven from the heart; the second interpretation's Postcommunion follows Augustine on Ps 84.4, its Collect states Bellarmine's and Chrysostom's ground, and the closing 'lessons in a time of waiting' subsection is removed, its Epistle and Gospel placed at Jerome's patientiam gloss and at the letter's seventy years.

First interpretation adds the Introit's invocabitis me (Jerome on Jer 29:7, same letter), the Collect (after Aquinas's liberantur a Deo) and the Postcommunion (Augustine's 'may it only find you wheat'); third adds the Gradual (Chrysostom on tota die, Expositio in Ps. 43 sec. 6), Postcommunion (Chrysostom's 'endureth to the end'), Introit (cogitationes pacis beside Chrysostom's umpire) and the Communion antiphon's own words (Bede on Mk 11:23, bound locus line 338); all ten texts verified in each of the three interpretations.

All cited sentences deleted or rewritten as required (40:33, 40:45-46, 40:66, 40:133-134 first sentence, 30:31, 20:52-54); also cut the restatements at 20:61-63, 20:226-227 and the two facts at 'How far correction may go', and a paraphrase of Bellarmine and Chrysostom in the second interpretation's Collect sentence; 'the subjects too' quoted once in the third interpretation.

'From this he draws his own conclusion' removed; q. 11 a. 3 re-read in the bound English Dominican text and given with its grounds (the sin, graver than forging money; mercy with two admonitions, then the salvation of others; Jerome on Gal 5:9), the parable answered in ad 3 by the reading of q. 10 a. 8 ad 1. The comparison states the position in the same terms, without the conditional reading as premise and without grading.

The hinge now grounds each hearer's field in Rabanus's seed of good will, states the Lord's gloss on the seed (Mt 13:38) and Aquinas's adherence to it (Super Mt. c. 13, 'accipitur ipse homo, in quo seminatur'), and makes the indwelling word what keeps the field, with Chrysostom's Scriptures as arms as the reason; the allegorical sense follows the gloss and credits Chrysostom and Aquinas only with the dwelling word, and the anagogy gathers the children of the kingdom.
